sections.h2: What is Lafayette Parish, and which towns does it include?
sections.html:
Lafayette Parish is a small parish in Acadiana, covering 269 square miles of almost entirely dry land. Wikipedia ranks it the fifth smallest parish in Louisiana by land area.

Six municipalities sit inside it. Lafayette is the parish seat and largest city, and the others are Broussard (partly in St. Martin Parish), Carencro, Scott, Youngsville and the town of Duson (partly in Acadia Parish). Milton and Ossun are census-designated places with no city government of their own.

The distinction matters for tax, because a house in Youngsville, Scott or Carencro is billed differently from a house in the City of Lafayette or in unincorporated parish land. Before you read a bill, confirm which municipality, if any, taxes your address.

sections.h2: How does the Sheriff's tax department collect in Lafayette Parish?
sections.html:
The Lafayette Parish Sheriff's Office mails roughly 100,000 property tax notices every November. Its tax department states that the deadline to pay without penalty is December 31 each year.

The office does more than bill the parish. In 2004 it merged tax collection with Carencro and Youngsville, and in 2008 it added Scott and Duson. Their bills combine local and parish taxes into one payment, and the Sheriff disburses the funds to each government afterward. If you live in one of those five places, you can send a single check.

  • Payment methods: cash, personal check or credit card, and online through the Sheriff's Web Tax Site.
  • Hours: Monday to Thursday 7:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., Friday 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m.
  • Online fees: the Consolidated Government says e-check and card payments carry a transaction fee.

The City of Lafayette is the exception. It bills its own city tax, so a house inside the city may need two payments.

sections.h2: What does the Lafayette Parish Assessor actually do?
sections.html:
The Assessor finds and values property, and has very little say over how much tax you pay. The office describes its job as identifying, locating and fairly valuing all real and personal property in the parish. The taxing bodies, including the city-parish government, school board and sheriff, set the rates that turn that value into a bill.

State law requires reassessment at least every four years, although a value can change annually when sales move the market. The Assessor uses the sales comparison approach first, then cost and income approaches as checks, and keeps a GIS parcel map, ownership records and building descriptions. The site offers a tax estimator and a property search, and the office phone is (337) 291-7080.

Sellers can use the property search to see their own assessment before they talk to a buyer. A fair assessment and a fair price are different things, but a wide gap is worth asking about.

sections.h2: What relief programs does Lafayette Parish offer homeowners?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption is the most widely used break. It covers up to 160 acres with an owner-occupied residence and exempts $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, from state, parish and special taxes. It also applies to a pool, pool house or storage building belonging to the owner, but not to a second house or commercial building on the same land.

A separate assessed value freeze is available to qualifying owners. The Assessor says the freeze locks the assessed value at its January 1, 2025 level until the home is sold or remodeled, and it ends on the last day of December of the year before a sale. Eligibility requires a homestead exemption on the property and one of these:

  • Age 65 or older.
  • A permanent, total disability determined by a court, state or federal agency.
  • A service-connected veteran disability rating of 50% or more.

Adjusted gross income must be $100,000 or less. Taxes can still rise, because the millage rate can change even when the assessed value is frozen. Agricultural land can be assessed on use value if it is at least three acres or has produced at least $2,000 in gross income in each of the preceding four years.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Lafayette Parish assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to a deputy assessor first, with evidence. To win a reduction you must show that the assessment is above market value and explain why. If you accept the deputy's answer, nothing more is required.

If you disagree, the Assessor's site says you may appeal to the Lafayette Consolidated Council during hearings held in September, with dates set by the Council in August. The Council reviews your material and the Assessor's information and rules at the hearing. A further appeal goes to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and Commission decisions are final unless appealed to district court within thirty days.

The current board's name and the exact filing cutoff were not confirmed on the pages we opened, because the city and parish councils were separated in 2018. Ask the Assessor for the filing date each summer.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid taxes in Lafayette Parish?
sections.html:
Taxes unpaid after the December 31 deadline accrue interest, and a house can eventually be sold at the annual tax sale, held online on the first Wednesday in June. Under the Louisiana Constitution, property sold at tax sale can be redeemed for three years after recordation by paying the price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest.

Properties that nobody buys at the sale are called adjudicated. Lafayette Consolidated Government's disposition process lets someone apply for one only after three consecutive years of adjudication. A public bid starts at a minimum of 75% of the Assessor's fair market value, and a second round, about a month later, starts at 33%. Outstanding taxes and liens are waived when the correct affidavit is recorded, and applicants are urged to hire an attorney with title experience.

The owner can redeem at any time until the act of sale to the applicant is recorded, by paying all taxes, liens and fees to both the city and the Sheriff. For a seller, that is the clearest reason to resolve arrears before they turn into an adjudication.

sections.h2: How does a sale with taxes owed work in Lafayette Parish?
sections.html:
Taxes owed are settled from the proceeds when the house sells. A closing agent can request a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901, which shows whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are paid, except those for the year of the sale.

A cash sale avoids the delay that comes with a buyer's mortgage and appraisal. Tax bills, inherited homes, tenants and repairs are the situations where speed helps. After closing, the buyer files a new homestead claim and the Assessor updates ownership, which the office tracks as part of its parcel work.

The act itself must be recorded with the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court. See our clerk of court guide for fees and steps.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Lafayette Parish?
faqs.a: The Lafayette Parish Sheriff's Office tax department mails about 100,000 notices each November and collects payments. The City of Lafayette bills its own city tax separately.

faqs.q: What is the Lafayette Parish tax deadline?
faqs.a: The Sheriff's deadline for paying without penalty is December 31 each year. Unpaid amounts then accrue interest and can lead to the tax sale in June.

faqs.q: What is the Lafayette Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It exempts $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home on up to 160 acres. The owner claims it with the Assessor.

faqs.q: Can seniors freeze their Lafayette Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Owners 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, can apply for an assessed value freeze if they hold a homestead exemption and have adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less. The freeze fixes the January 1, 2025 value.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Lafayette Parish house with back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Selling before adjudication keeps you in control of the property and stops interest from growing.
